title: Design Patterns for AI Trust: Juries, Libraries, and Agent Tiers — Alex Bauer, Upside.tech

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core subject is agent harness architecture—scaffolding with anchor assets, a librarian consult pattern, and a multi-agent jury-and-judge loop are all control-plane design around a model. The patterns are applied to go-to-market workflows including pipeline, attribution, and revenue data at an enterprise-operations company whose product is a data-and-analytics layer. Coverage spans designing agent patterns, building scaffolding and anchor assets, and selecting appropriate model tiers for deployment. The audience spans engineers to non-coders, and the patterns are conveyed through accessible metaphors and live demos rather than deep technical internals. This is a conference talk delivered with slides, live demonstrations, and real production failure case studies. Multiple direct transcript quotes anchor each classification claim with specific evidence IDs drawn from the supplied analysis.

summary: Alex Bauer opens with a bedtime story metaphor: a go-to-market team quests to understand their business, facing monsters representing security reviews, data silos with conflicting definitions, and the hardest question of all. Each story element maps to a real problem he then addresses practically. Bauer introduces Upside.tech as the data layer for agentic GTM, helping teams prepare data for AI, prevent hallucination, and make data accessible wherever needed. The talk's core thesis is that AI has made everyone technical enough to be dangerous, turning non-builders into builders. But this power surfaces a trust problem: AI doesn't say I'm not sure—it gives wrong answers that look exactly like right ones. Bauer's solution is manage agents like humans. Use commander's intent (from military doctrine) in prompts—tell agents why, not just what—because models trained on human material tend to micromanage themselves. The first example is a website rebuild that would have taken two months at his previous 600-person company. YOLO mode failed even with Claude plan mode. The fix was scaffolding: maintaining anchor assets like a product capabilities reference with citations proving the AI didn't hallucinate critical details. He also describes Persona Bench—a set of agents inhabiting key personas who review work on demand. The second pattern is the radiant librarian: when a user asks something like how much pipeline did we create in Q1, the agent consults the librarian first. The librarian has access to documentation, knowledge items, and the schema of prior failed queries, preventing naive mistakes like interpreting Q1 as a simple date range. The librarian provides just-in-time memory—knowing fiscal year starts in February, pipeline means stage two or later—yielding trustworthy answers with citations. The third pattern is jury-and-judge: for questions with no empirically correct answer, like multi-touch attribution (which took two years to approach), the agent spins up independent analysts who each produce evidence-cited opinions. A consensus judge weighs reasoning quality rather than treating outputs as fact, escalating and expanding the jury if consensus is insufficient. The bonus section covers agent tiers: Bauer warns against using low-intelligence models for important work, citing Slackbot's MCP integration as 'horrifically stupid' because subscription-plan margins don't support intelligent reasoning. He recommends at least tier-two models with sub-agents, plan mode, full MCP support, and file editing.

sections.title: Opening & Bedtime Story Metaphor
sections.summary: Bauer opens with audience participation and a personal anecdote about his newborn son. He then tells a bedtime story framing a GTM team's quest to understand their business, facing monsters: a security guardian defeated with paperwork, a many-headed monster of conflicting definitions requiring building a unified data layer, and a final boss that asks the hardest question. The story's resolution—write down how your world works, give adventurers a knowledgeable guide, let them teach each other—previews the talk's real patterns.

sections.title: Agenda & Company Introduction
sections.summary: Bauer transitions from the story to the real talk, explaining each story element maps to a real problem. He introduces Upside.tech as the data layer for agentic GTM: helping teams prepare data for AI, answer previously impossible questions at scale, prevent hallucination, and make data accessible wherever teams want to use it.

sections.title: The Age of Agentic GTM
sections.summary: Bauer explains how AI has transformed GTM teams. Historically, marketers and salespeople weren't builders—their tools were spreadsheets and PowerPoint. AI changes this, making building accessible like the bicycle did for mobility. He categorizes the audience into engineers, those technical enough to be dangerous, and non-coders, noting AI makes everyone technical enough to be dangerous with an infinite supply of valedictorian interns.

sections.title: Trust Problem & Core Thesis
sections.summary: Bauer reframes the hallucination problem as its older sibling: a trust problem. AI won't say 'I'm not sure'—it gives wrong answers that look exactly like right ones. His central thesis: when in doubt, manage agents like other humans. The one practical tip: use commander's intent in prompts—tell agents why you want something done. Beware that agents trained on human material micromanage themselves.

sections.title: Example 1: Website Rebuild & Scaffolding
sections.summary: Bauer needed to redo his company's entire website—previously a 2-month multi-person effort at his 600-person company. YOLO mode failed even with Claude plan mode. The fix was scaffolding: maintaining anchor assets including a product capabilities reference with citations proving AI didn't hallucinate, general DSLO scale references, and Persona Bench agents that review work on demand. Define structure first, then turn Claude loose.

sections.title: The Radiant Librarian Pattern
sections.summary: Bauer introduces the radiant librarian, a pattern built into Upside's product. When a user asks something like 'How much pipeline did we create in Q1?', the agent consults the librarian first rather than naively interpreting the query. The librarian has access to documentation, knowledge items about the company, and the schema of prior failed queries—giving the agent a knowledgeable guide, analogous to onboarding a new hire. The librarian provides just-in-time memory: knowing fiscal year starts in February, pipeline means stage two or later. Output is a trustworthy answer with citations rather than something discovered for the first time.

sections.title: Example 3: Jury-and-Judge Workflow
sections.summary: Bauer presents the jury-and-judge pattern for questions with no empirically correct answer, using multi-touch attribution as the example. Upside was founded to solve multi-touch attribution; it took 2 years to get close, but along the way they built an AI-native data layer that turned out to be what everyone needed. Enabled by Opus, the jury workflow spins up independent analysts who each examine data and produce evidence-cited opinions on attribution credit. A consensus judge weighs reasoning quality rather than treating outputs as fact, escalating and expanding the jury if consensus is insufficient. This mirrors how humans handle high-stakes subjective calls—multiple researchers plus a synthesizer beats one person perseverating.

sections.title: Bonus: Agent Tiers & Closing
sections.summary: Bauer adds a bonus on agent tiers: 'you can't fix stupid.' Don't use bad harnesses or low-intelligence models for important work. He cites Slackbot's newly released MCP client as 'horrifically stupid' because subscription-plan margins can't support intelligent reasoning models. He recommends at least tier-two models with sub-agents, plan mode, full MCP support, and file editing—don't let teams rely on ChatGPT web interface for important work. He closes by pointing to Jeff from xAI's upcoming talk and offering to take questions outside.
